claims.text: Elevated chromium content enhances formation of a stable chromium oxide layer on corrosion-resistant steels.
Minor molybdenum additions enhance formation of the protective oxide layer.
The chromium oxide layer is self-healing.
The chromium oxide layer acts as a barrier against corrosive species.
Oxidation of chromium-enriched steels produces a uniform, adherent Cr2O3 film.
The Cr2O3 film physically blocks chlorides and other corrosive species from attacking the underlying metal.
A disrupted passive film can self-heal when sufficient chromium is available.
Higher-chromium steels will form thicker protective oxide layers than lower-chromium baseline steels.
Higher-chromium steels will form more uniform protective oxide layers than lower-chromium baseline steels.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit lower corrosion rates than lower-chromium baseline steels under identical conditions.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit greater electrochemical impedance than lower-chromium baseline steels.
Higher-chromium steels will exhibit lower pitting density than lower-chromium baseline steels.
Lower-chromium steels with minimal molybdenum will form thinner and less protective oxide films.
Lower-chromium steels with minimal molybdenum will have higher corrosion rates.
The proposed mechanism should operate at moderate temperatures, under controlled oxidative atmospheres, and at low to moderate mechanical stress.
At temperatures above 300°C, the protective oxide film may degrade or spall.
High mechanical stress may cause the protective-oxide mechanism to cease applying.
